strategies.name: Carshare
strategies.short_description: Availability of shared vehicles for short-term use as an alternative to personal car ownership.
strategies.extended_description:
Carshare programs provide members access to shared vehicles for short-term use, billed by
the hour or trip, as an alternative to owning a personal vehicle. By making it practical to
live with fewer (or no) household vehicles, carshare nudges members toward transit, walking,
biking, and as-needed driving, reducing overall vehicle miles traveled.

The effect of carshare depends on how many residents join and how readily transit and
active modes can serve their everyday trips. Carshare is most effective in compact,
mixed-use areas with good transit and parking pressure, where the cost and hassle of car
ownership are highest and members can comfortably go car-light or car-free.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy where a project supports access to shared vehicles, such as
round-trip or one-way carshare pods, dedicated parking, or partnerships with a carshare
operator. Carshare works best alongside density, transit, and parking-management
strategies.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-21 (structural; constants pending fact-sheet confirmation)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Carshare reduces vehicle miles traveled (VMT) primarily by lowering private vehicle
ownership and shifting members toward as-needed vehicle access, transit, and active modes,
following CAPCOA
[T-21 (Implement Carshare Program)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-21.pdf).
The credit is the share of the service-area population who become members times the
per-member VMT reduction, capped at the Neighborhood Design subsector maximum (10%):

`ΔVMT% = −min(participation_rate × service_area_share × member_vmt_reduction, 10%)`

> **Constants pending confirmation.** The verbatim T-21 equation and its default constants
> (member participation rate, per-member VMT reduction, measure maximum) were not captured
> during research, and the T-21 fact sheet was unreachable at implementation time. The
> participation rate and per-member reduction are **placeholders** exposed in the code
> (`CARSHARE_T21`) for recalibration and should be confirmed against the T-21 fact sheet
> before the numeric results are relied upon. The structural form is unit-consistent and
> the result is bounded by the subsector cap. Outputs flag this assumption.

**Sources**

- CAPCOA *Handbook* (2021), Measure
  [T-21 (Implement Carshare Program)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-21.pdf)
  (also published as T-21-A Conventional and T-21-B Electric).

applicability.warn_message: Carshare has a measurable effect mainly in compact, transit-served areas; results use placeholder constants pending CAPCOA T-21 confirmation.

inputs.label: Share of area within carshare service area
inputs.summary: The share of the area's residents who live within walking distance of a shared vehicle or carshare pod.
inputs.source_note: your carshare program plan / operator service-area map
inputs.tooltip: Share of the area's population living within the carshare service area (walking distance of a shared vehicle).
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of the area's residents who live within the carshare service area,
roughly walking distance of a shared vehicle or pod. Use 100% if the whole area is
served; lower it for a pilot covering only part of the area.

strategies.name: Commuter Incentives
strategies.short_description: Financial or non-financial rewards (transit benefits, rideshare subsidies, prizes) that pay employees to shift out of driving alone.
strategies.extended_description:
Commuter incentives provide a financial or other tangible benefit for changing travel
behavior. The incentive may support transit use, carpooling, vanpooling, bicycling,
telework, remote parking, or another specific action, but it should be tied to a
measurable change rather than general awareness.

The effect is strongest when incentives support repeated behavior or change the relative
cost of driving alone. Short-term incentives can encourage commuters to try a new mode,
while recurring benefits, like free transit passes provided by employers for example,
are more likely to influence ongoing commute choices.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for incentive-driven programs. For awareness and
promotion without payments, use [Commute Trip Reduction
Marketing](#/strategies/commute_marketing).
Avoid double-counting if an overlapping fare subsidy or parking cash-out is also modeled
for the same commuters.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-5 / T-6 (Commute Trip Reduction), incentive-heavy ≈3%
strategies.methodology_detail:
Incentive-heavy commute programs reduce commute VMT by roughly 3% per eligible
commuter, drawn from the commute-trip-reduction evidence in CAPCOA
[T-5 (voluntary)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-5.pdf)
and [T-6 (mandatory)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-6.pdf).
Programs that pair financial incentives with outreach land toward the upper end
of that range:

`Δcommute_VMT% = −%eligible × reduction_per_eligible`

Adjust the per-commuter rate to match the level of incentives antcipated in the program.

inputs.label: Share of workforce eligible
inputs.summary: The share of area employees eligible for the incentive program. For a single employer this is its share of area commuters; for a regional program, use the eligible workforce share.
inputs.source_note: your project scope / employer or program participation estimate
inputs.tooltip: Share of area employees eligible for the incentives.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of area employees eligible for the incentive program. For a
single employer, this is its share of area commuters; for a regional program,
estimate the eligible workforce share.

inputs.label: Reduction per eligible commuter
inputs.summary: The commute-VMT reduction per eligible commuter. Keep 3% for incentive-heavy programs, or lower toward 1-2% for token incentives.
inputs.source_note: CAPCOA T-5/T-6 default (3%); adjust from your program's incentive level
inputs.tooltip: 3% = incentive-heavy default. Lower to 1-2% for light incentives.
inputs.instructions:
The default 3% reflects programs with meaningful financial incentives. Lower it
toward 1-2% for token incentives.

strategies.notes: Split from commute_program. Engine: strategy_commute_program (incentive default ~3%).

strategies.name: Commute Trip Reduction Marketing
strategies.short_description: Outreach, information, and promotion encouraging employees to try alternative-mode commutes.
strategies.extended_description:
Commute trip reduction marketing is a planned outreach effort that connects a defined
audience with transportation options they can realistically use. These campaigns can
support new or existing services by helping people understand how to take the next step,
such as using transit, joining a vanpool, or biking to work.

Marketing works best when the message is tied to clear travel options. Broad awareness
alone is unlikely to change travel behavior if the alternative is inconvenient, unclear,
or unsupported by high quality multimodal infrastructure, transit service, incentives,
or other tangible TDM measures.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for information- and promotion-driven programs. When the
program provides payments, subsidies, rewards, or prizes to encourage mode shift, use
[Commuter
Incentives](#/strategies/commute_incentives)
instead.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-7 (Commute Trip Reduction Marketing), marketing-only ≈1%
strategies.methodology_detail:
Marketing-only commute programs reduce commute VMT by roughly 1% per reached
commuter ([CAPCOA T-7, Implement Commute Trip Reduction Marketing](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-7.pdf), low end):

`Δcommute_VMT% = −%reached × reduction_per_reached`

Adjust the per-commuter rate if local evaluation supports a different value.

inputs.label: Share of workforce reached
inputs.summary: The share of area employees reached by the marketing/outreach program. For a single employer this is its share of area commuters; for a regional campaign, use the workforce share.
inputs.source_note: your project scope / marketing campaign reach estimate
inputs.tooltip: Share of area employees at workplaces running the marketing program.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of area employees who work at sites participating in the
marketing/outreach program. For a single employer, this is its share of area
commuters; for a regional campaign, estimate the share of the workforce impacted by the program.

inputs.label: Reduction per reached commuter
inputs.summary: The commute-VMT reduction per reached commuter. Keep the 1% marketing-only default unless local program evaluation supports a higher value.
inputs.source_note: CAPCOA T-7 default (1%); raise only with local program evaluation
inputs.tooltip: 1% = marketing based program default (CAPCOA T-7 low end). Raise only with local evidence.
inputs.instructions:
The default 1% reflects marketing/outreach-only programs. Increase it only if
local program evaluation documents a stronger response; stronger results
usually come from pairing outreach with incentives. For more benefits see the Commute-trip reduction incentives strategy.

strategies.notes: Split from commute_program. Engine: strategy_commute_program (marketing default ~1%).

strategies.name: Dynamic Parking Pricing
strategies.short_description: Adjust parking prices by demand, time, or location; estimated from the resulting average price drivers pay.
strategies.extended_description:
Dynamic parking pricing adjusts rates by time of day, location, observed occupancy, or
other factors. The purpose is to keep some spaces available in high-demand areas, reduce
time spent searching for parking, and encourage commuters to consider other travel
options when appropriate.

The additional effect of dynamic pricing can be difficult to separate from parking
pricing generally, so results should be interpreted as approximate.
strategies.guidance:
Handy et al. (2025) advise against treating dynamic pricing as a distinct
measure because its added effect beyond parking pricing is difficult to isolate. When in
doubt, model the average price under [Parking Fees and Curb
Management](#/strategies/parking_fees_curb_management)
instead.
strategies.method: Lehner & Peer (2019) parking elasticity (ε=−0.40) on average price (effect-size estimate)
strategies.methodology_detail:
What reduces driving is the average price drivers pay, not the fact that the price
varies. This strategy is therefore estimated the same way as fixed parking fees, using
the average resulting price. Raising that average price raises the cost of driving
to those destinations and reduces vehicle miles traveled (VMT), following CAPCOA
[T-24 (Implement Market Price Public Parking, On-Street)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-24.pdf)
and the parking-response relationship in Lehner & Peer (2019).

`ΔVMT% = %Δprice × ε × share_affected`

Because Handy et al. (2025) do not recommend estimating dynamic pricing on its
own, treat the result as a rough estimate only.

applicability.warn_message: Demand-responsive pricing applies where parking demand is high (urban downtowns and districts) and is rarely relevant at lower densities.

inputs.label: Average resulting price
inputs.summary: The average full-day price drivers will pay under the demand-responsive scheme (across times and locations), not the peak rate.
inputs.source_note: your proposed pricing schedule / parking rate policy
inputs.tooltip: Average price drivers pay under the dynamic scheme. The starting price defaults to the typical price for this type of area.
inputs.instructions:
Enter the average price drivers will pay under the dynamic scheme (a full-day
equivalent across times and locations), not the peak rate. If parking is free
today, any new average price is treated as a meaningful increase.

inputs.label: Share of area VMT priced
inputs.summary: The share of the area's driving whose destinations fall within the demand-responsive pricing zone.
inputs.source_note: your pricing-zone boundary vs. area travel patterns
inputs.tooltip: Share of the area's driving whose destinations fall under the dynamic pricing.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of the area's driving whose destinations fall within the
dynamic pricing zone. This input is required.

strategies.notes: Promoted from todo; split from the pricing engine. Engine: strategy_parking_pricing (trip_purpose=all). Handy 2025: standalone quantification not recommended.

strategies.name: Employee Commuting Benefits
strategies.short_description: Employer- or development-provided subsidized/free transit passes (ECO passes) and commute benefits, scoped to commute travel.
strategies.extended_description:
Employee commuting benefits reduce the cost or inconvenience of commuting without
driving alone. Benefits may include employer-provided transit passes, vanpool support,
commuter incentives, workplace bicycle amenities, flexible work options, or other
assistance that makes non-drive-alone commuting easier.

The effectiveness of this strategy depends on how well the benefit matches employee
travel needs. Transit passes work best with high quality, frequent, and accessible
transit. These benefits can also be paired with clear promotion of benefits and other
TDM measures that make non-single-occupancy vehicle modes more appealing.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for employer- or development-provided commute benefits,
such as an RTD EcoPass or other pass or subsidy program. For a general transit pass
subsidy that is not tied to a worksite or development, use [Transit Pass
Subsidies](#/strategies/transit_pass_subsidy).
Avoid double-counting if parking cash-out or [Commuter
Incentives](#/strategies/commute_incentives)
are modeled for the same commuters.
strategies.method: Paulley (2006) fare elasticity (ε=−0.30), commute scope
strategies.formula: Δcommute_VMT% = (Δfare × eligible × ε × transit_MS × 1/AVO × p_drive) / auto_MS
strategies.methodology_detail:
Same short-run fare elasticity as the general pass subsidy (ε = −0.30, Paulley
et al. 2006), here implementing CAPCOA
[T-9 (Implement Subsidized or Discounted Transit Program)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-9.pdf),
scoped to commute VMT and discounted by the share of benefiting commuters who
would otherwise drive:

`Δcommute_VMT% = (Δfare × eligible × ε × transit_MS × 1/AVO × p_drive) / auto_MS`

When the benefit is entered as a dollar subsidy, the effective fare reduction is
the subsidy divided by the average fare (statewide default unless provided).
Mode share comes from the American Community Survey (ACS); Average vehicle occupancy is from the 2017 National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) statewide default.

applicability.warn_message: Transit commute benefits depend on employees having a usable transit option, which is limited in rural areas.

inputs.label: Monthly/trip subsidy value
inputs.summary: The per-trip dollar value of the commute benefit; if you have a monthly pass value, divide by the typical monthly commute transit trips to get a per-trip figure.
inputs.source_note: your employer or development's transit benefit (ECO pass / subsidy) offering
inputs.tooltip: Dollar value of the commute benefit per transit trip; converted to an effective fare reduction.
inputs.instructions:
Enter the per-trip dollar value of the commute benefit (the calculator
converts it to a fare reduction using the average fare). If your benefit is a
monthly pass value, divide by the typical number of commute transit trips per
month to get a per-trip figure.

inputs.label: Share of commuters eligible
inputs.summary: The share of area commuters offered the benefit. For a single employer this is its share of area commuters; for a development requirement, use the share at the affected sites.
inputs.source_note: your project scope / employer or development participation estimate
inputs.tooltip: Share of area commuters offered the benefit.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of area commuters offered the benefit. For a single
employer, this is its share of area commuters; for a development requirement,
estimate the share of commuters at the affected sites.

strategies.notes: Promoted from todo; split from the fare engine. Engine: strategy_transit_fare_subsidy (scope=commute).

compute.formula: pct_fare_reduction * pct_eligible * elasticity * transit_mode_share * (1 / avo) / max(auto_mode_share, 0.000000001) * pct_otherwise_drive

strategies.name: Increased Employment Density
strategies.short_description: Increase jobs per acre (including mixed-use intensification) to shorten trips and support non-auto commuting.
strategies.extended_description:
Increasing employment density concentrates jobs, stores, and services closer together
and closer to residents. Shorter distances can make walking, bicycling, and transit more
practical and can reduce the amount of driving required for daily activities.

The effect is strongest when added jobs or services are located in a mixed-use context
with safe walking and bicycling conditions. The same number of jobs in an isolated
office park, for example, will generally have less effect if most trips still require a
car.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for job-focused or mixed-use development. To model a
project that adds both homes and jobs, or a broader change in land use mix, combine it
with [Increased Residential
Density](#/strategies/residential_density).
strategies.method: Stevens (2016) employment VMT-density elasticity (ε=−0.07)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Adding jobs and destinations to an area shortens trips and makes walking, biking,
and transit more practical, which lowers vehicle miles traveled (VMT). A 1%
increase in employment density has been associated with about a 0.07% reduction
in VMT (Stevens 2016), the basis CAPCOA uses for
[T-2 (Increase Job Density)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-2.pdf).
Job density is a weaker lever than housing density, so the percentage is smaller.

`ΔVMT% = Δemp_density × ε_emp`

To represent a change in the mix of land uses or a mixed-use development, combine
this strategy with Increase residential density.

applicability.warn_message: The density–driving relationship comes from urban and suburban areas; in rural areas, added density yields little reduction in driving.

inputs.label: Change in employment density
inputs.summary: The percent change in jobs per acre the project adds, compared with today's baseline for the project area.
inputs.source_note: your development program / site plan vs. local baseline job density
inputs.tooltip: Proposed job density vs. today's baseline.
inputs.benchmark: Jobs/sq mi: suburban office park ~5,000–15,000; dense urban district ~30,000–50,000; downtown Denver core ~60,000.
inputs.instructions:
Enter the percentage change in job density compared with today's baseline for
the project area. A project that doubles job density is +100%.

Approximate benchmarks (jobs per square mile):

- Suburban office park or commercial: ~5,000–15,000
- Dense urban employment district: ~30,000–50,000
- Downtown Denver office core: ~60,000

These are order-of-magnitude anchors; local figures vary with how tightly the
district is drawn.

strategies.notes: Split from density_change. Engine: strategy_density_change (pct_change_res_density=0).

strategies.name: Workplace Bicycle Amenities
strategies.short_description: Workplace bike parking, showers, and lockers that raise bike commute mode share by a documented effect size.
strategies.extended_description:
Workplace bicycle amenities provide secure bicycle parking, lockers, showers, changing
rooms, repair stations, or similar amenities for employees. These amenities address
common barriers that can keep employees from considering biking as a commute option.

The effect depends on whether employees live within a reasonable bicycling distance and
whether the surrounding bike network provides a comfortable and direct connection to the
worksite. Amenities at a worksite near safe, connected bicycle routes will generally
have a stronger effect than the same amenities at a site that is not close to
high-quality bike facilities that are part of a larger bike network.
strategies.guidance:
This is a workplace measure, led by an employer or developer, that applies
to commute trips. For area-wide on-street bicycle infrastructure, use [Striped Bike
Lanes, Neighborhood Bikeways and
Sharrows](#/strategies/sharrows_bike_lanes)
or [Protected or Buffered Bike
Lanes](#/strategies/separated_bike_lanes)
instead.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-10 (Provide End-of-Trip Bicycle Facilities), commute scope
strategies.methodology_detail:
Showers, lockers, and secure bike parking remove a common reason people don't bike
to work, leading more employees to bike for their commute and lowering commute
vehicle miles traveled (VMT). Providing these facilities raises the share of
commute trips made by bike by about 5% among employees who have access, following
CAPCOA
[T-10 (Provide End-of-Trip Bicycle Facilities)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-10.pdf).
Because bike trips are shorter than car trips, the calculator accounts for that
when converting added bike commutes into driving avoided.

`Δcommute_VMT% = −scope_share × L_bike × (bike_MS × adj) / (L_veh × auto_MS)`

This applies the same bike effect as [Striped Bike Lanes, Neighborhood Bikeways and
Sharrows](https://high-street.bitbucket.io/cdot_tdm_calculator/#/strategies/sharrows_bike_lanes),
focused on commuters at a worksite rather than across an area.

applicability.warn_message: Biking to work is most practical at denser, bike-served worksites; the effect is limited in rural areas.

inputs.label: Share of commuters with access
inputs.summary: The share of commuters in your area who work at sites that will provide end-of-trip bicycle facilities such as secure parking, showers, and lockers.
inputs.source_note: your employer roster or development standards / site plans
inputs.tooltip: Share of area commuters at workplaces that provide end-of-trip facilities.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of commuters in your project area who work at sites that
will provide end-of-trip facilities. For a single large employer, this is the
employer's share of area commuters; for a development standard applied to new
workplaces, estimate the share of commuters those sites represent.

strategies.notes: Split from bike_mode_share_booster. Engine: strategy_bike_mode_share_booster (scope=commute).

strategies.name: Increased Transit Service
strategies.short_description: New routes, route extensions, or expanded operating hours for an existing transit network, giving more people a transit option.
strategies.extended_description:
Increased transit service introduces transit access where it was not previously available
or extends service to new markets. This may include a new local route, an extension of an
existing route, or a new regional connection. This may also include expanding operating
hours. The service is most useful when it links people to jobs, schools, services, or
activity centers at times that match actual travel needs.

The effect of increased transit service depends on how many riders the service attracts
and how many of those trips would otherwise have been made by driving alone. Increased
service is most likely to reduce VMT where it connects places people already need to
travel, offers reliable travel times, and offers connectivity between transit stops and
final destinations.

This strategy models **fixed-route** transit service (scheduled routes along a fixed
alignment). Demand-responsive services such as microtransit and on-demand circulators
are modeled separately and are not included here.
strategies.guidance:
Use this when a project expands fixed-route service, such as new routes, route
extensions, regional connections, or expanded operating hours. To increase how often existing
routes run, use [Transit Service Frequency Increase](#/strategies/transit_service_expansion)
instead.
strategies.method: TCRP 95 service-miles elasticity (ε=0.75)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Extending transit into new areas gives more people a usable alternative to
driving, so some car trips shift to transit and vehicle miles traveled (VMT) fall.
The more service is added relative to what exists today, the larger the ridership
gain. This follows CAPCOA
[T-25 (Extend Transit Network Coverage or Hours)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-25.pdf)
and the service-miles relationship in Transit Cooperative Research Program (TCRP)
Report 95.

`ΔVMT% = −L × Δservice × transit_MS × ε × (1/AVO) × trip_reduction_ratio`

The calculator uses local commute mode share from the American Community Survey
(ACS) and a statewide average for vehicle occupancy (the average number of people
per car), and it discounts for new transit trips that don't fully replace a car
trip. Use the implementation level to phase in service that isn't fully running
yet.

applicability.warn_message: New transit coverage reduces the most driving where density supports ridership; expect a limited effect in rural areas.

inputs.label: Service-mile change
inputs.summary: The percent change in revenue miles the new or extended service adds, compared with the existing network serving your area.
inputs.tooltip: Signed: positive = added revenue miles / new routes, negative = a service cut.
inputs.instructions:
Enter the percentage change in transit revenue miles for the affected area.
Compare the daily (or annual) revenue miles of the new/extended service
against the existing network serving the area. For a brand-new route in an
area with little prior service, this can be large; for a modest extension it
may be a few percent.

To check the existing routes, operators, and service in your area, CDOT's
[Statewide Transit Routes map](https://cdot.maps.arcgis.com/apps/mapviewer/index.html?layers=dd812c7abb8e4017bc83e2cf9ef54824)
maps fixed-route transit statewide.

inputs.label: Implementation level
inputs.summary: What share of the planned service will actually be operating. Use 100% for a full build-out, less for a pilot or phased roll-out.
inputs.source_note: your project scope / agency service plan
inputs.tooltip: Phase-in factor. 100% = the new/expanded service is fully operating.
inputs.instructions:
Use this to phase in the effect. 100% means the new or expanded service is
fully operating across the impacted area; a pilot or partial roll-out lowers it.

To check the existing routes, operators, and service in your area, CDOT's
[Statewide Transit Routes map](https://cdot.maps.arcgis.com/apps/mapviewer/index.html?layers=dd812c7abb8e4017bc83e2cf9ef54824)
maps fixed-route transit statewide.

strategies.name: Lane Miles Added (Negative Impact on VMT)
strategies.short_description: Change in roadway capacity. Added lanes increase VMT via induced demand; a road diet (negative lane miles) reduces it. Magnitude depends on facility class.
strategies.extended_description:
Adding lane miles is an inverse measure that estimates potential VMT increases. Unlike
the other measures in this tool, adding lane miles is not seen as a TDM strategy. For
the purposes of this tool, this estimate measures the potential negative impacts
associated with added lane miles and induced demand.

The effect of induced demand will vary by roadway type and context, with major freeway
capacity typically producing stronger induced travel effects than small changes on
lower-volume streets.

This same relationship runs in reverse: removing through-lane capacity (a **road
diet**) reduces VMT. To model a road diet, enter a **negative** number of lane miles
(e.g. `-2` for a project that removes two lane-miles of general-purpose capacity).
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy to estimate added driving from a roadway capacity
project, or VMT savings from a road diet (enter negative lane miles). Apply it to
general-purpose capacity changes; specialized improvements such as turn lanes, bus-only
lanes, or safety projects should be evaluated based on their specific purpose.
strategies.method: Duranton & Turner 2011 long-run induced-demand elasticities
strategies.methodology_detail:
Widening a road or adding lanes makes driving easier, which over time generates
more vehicle miles traveled (VMT), an effect known as induced demand. The added
driving is proportional to how much the new lanes increase capacity for that type
of road.

`ΔVMT% = (new_lane_miles / existing_lane_miles_in_class) × ε`

The strength of the effect depends on the road type: freeways and expressways
bring out the most new travel, arterials less, and collectors and local streets
the least (Duranton & Turner 2011). Induced demand is not a CAPCOA reduction
measure, so no CAPCOA reference applies.

inputs.label: Net change in general-purpose lane miles
inputs.summary: The net change in through-lane miles the project makes (positive for added lanes, negative for a road diet), excluding turn lanes and shoulders.
inputs.source_note: your project scope / roadway design
inputs.tooltip: Signed net change in through-lane miles, excluding turn lanes and shoulders. Positive = lanes added; negative = a road diet (lanes removed).
inputs.instructions:
Enter the net change in through-lane miles the project makes: lane-miles, not
centerline miles (a 2-mile project adding one lane each way is 4 lane-miles).
Use a **positive** value for added capacity and a **negative** value to model a
**road diet** that removes through-lane capacity (e.g. `-4` for a 2-mile project
that removes one lane each way). Exclude turn lanes, auxiliary lanes, and shoulders.

inputs.label: Facility class
inputs.summary: The functional classification of the road being widened or narrowed; freeways induce the most new travel, local streets the least.
inputs.source_note: the functional class of the road in your project scope
inputs.tooltip: Sets how strongly new capacity brings out traffic. Existing lane miles for the area come from the loaded network.
inputs.instructions:
Pick the class of the road being widened. It sets how strongly the new capacity
brings out traffic: freeways and expressways induce the most new travel,
arterials less, and collectors and local streets the least. Match it to the
functional classification of the road you're expanding.

strategies.name: Mixed-Use Development (Without Transit)
strategies.short_description: Co-locating residential, commercial, office, civic, and recreational land uses in a single location, where the development is not tied to a high-quality transit station.
strategies.extended_description:
Mixed-use development permits residential, commercial, office, civic, and/or recreational
land uses in a single location. By locating housing, jobs, services, and daily needs closer
together, mixed-use development can reduce reliance on long single-occupancy vehicle trips.

The effect of mixed-use development will vary based on the specific land uses proposed,
density, street connectivity, parking conditions, and access to transit and active
transportation. Its VMT reduction potential may be lower where uses are technically mixed
but still separated by large blocks, wide roads, excessive parking, or limited pedestrian
and bicycle connections.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for land use projects or policies that bring complementary
uses closer together but are not specifically tied to high-quality transit. It is most
appropriate when housing, jobs, services, retail, civic uses, or recreation are co-located
so that some daily trips can be made by walking, biking, or shorter drives. For development
centered on a major transit station, use [Transit-Oriented
Development](#/strategies/transit_oriented_development)
instead.

strategies.name: Mobility hub
strategies.short_description: A central location where multiple travel modes (transit, bikeshare, micromobility, ride-hailing, etc.) connect seamlessly.
strategies.extended_description:
Mobility hubs connect multiple travel options in a convenient location, such as transit,
bikeshare, micromobility, rideshare, carshare, or shuttle services. Mobility hubs can help
users transfer between modes, complete first/last-mile connections, and reach destinations
that may be difficult to access by one mode alone.

The effect of a mobility hub will vary based on the number, quality, and usefulness of the
services connected through the hub. Mobility hubs are most effective when they link
reliable transportation options, serve key origins and destinations, and make transfers
between modes simple, visible, and convenient.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for projects that create or improve a location where
multiple travel options are intentionally connected, such as transit, bikeshare,
scooter-share, carshare, rideshare, shuttles, or secure bike parking. Mobility hubs should
be modeled where the hub improves access to useful services or destinations. Avoid
double-counting individual mobility components that are also modeled separately unless the
inputs are clearly separated.
strategies.notes: Tier 1. Sheet: quantification not recommended (Handy et al. 2025), but a composite-stack Python reference exists (strategy_mobility_hub).

strategies.name: Park-and-Ride
strategies.short_description: Designated parking facilities where travelers can leave personal vehicles and transfer to transit or carpools.
strategies.extended_description:
Park-and-rides are designated facilities where users can leave personal vehicles and
transfer to transit, carpools, vanpools, or shuttle services. Park-and-rides can support
longer commute trips, regional travel, first/last-mile access to transit, and connections
for users who do not live within walking or biking distance of frequent transit service.

The effect of a park-and-ride will vary based on its location, utilization, and connection
to useful transportation services. Park-and-rides are most effective when they are paired
with reliable transit, organized carpools or vanpools, frequent shuttle service, or managed
parking strategies, especially in suburban, rural, and regional corridor contexts where
they can shorten drive-alone trips rather than simply adding new vehicle trips to reach
transit.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for new or improved park-and-ride facilities that connect
drivers to various types of transit services. Park-and-rides are most appropriate when
users can replace a longer drive-alone trip with a shorter drive to a park-and-ride paired
with a transit trip.
strategies.method: Derived (Duncan & Cao 2020) with local TAZ catchment
strategies.methodology_detail:
A park-and-ride converts a would-be drive-all-the-way commute into a shorter drive to the
lot plus a transit trip. The credit is the avoided line-haul mileage, net of the access
drive, for the riders who would otherwise have driven the whole way. No CAPCOA measure or
CARB brief quantifies park-and-ride, so this method is built on the only US study that
isolates the *marginal* VMT effect (Duncan & Cao 2020), with the avoided mileage
reconstructed from local Colorado trip lengths.

**Spatial catchment.** Savings accrue along the corridor riders come from, not at the lot.
The calculator identifies the catchment (the Traffic Analysis Zones, or TAZs, within the
average access drive of the facility) and measures the reduction against the commute
vehicle miles traveled (VMT) *produced by those TAZs*.

**Binding constraint.** Diverted round trips are computed two ways and the lower (binding)
value is used:

- *Supply side* (parking capacity): `spaces × utilization × diversion_fraction`
- *Demand side* (who actually drives to transit): `transit_commute_trips × drive-to-transit share × diversion_fraction`

The drive-to-transit access share comes from the area's observed transit-access split (the
share of transit riders who reach transit by car versus on foot) rather than a national
default. The avoided VMT per diverted round trip is `V_net = 2 × (commute trip length −
access drive length)`, using the area's observed commute trip length. The diversion
fraction is 0.80 for an isolated facility and 0.32 where a comparable alternative exists
(Duncan & Cao 2020). Where local trip lengths are unavailable, the method falls back to
Duncan & Cao's empirical 19 mi (isolated) / 10 mi (alternative) per round trip, which
already embed the diversion behavior.

**Context limitation:** This method is defensible for the US auto-oriented commuter
context that matches Colorado. International studies (Mingardo 2013; Parkhurst 2000) find
park-and-ride can *increase* vehicle travel in some European settings; those are out of
scope here. Commute-VMT reductions above ~5% of the catchment are flagged for review.

**Sources**

- Duncan, M., & Cao, J. (2020). *Marginal Impacts of Park-and-Ride Facilities in the Twin
  Cities*. Transportation Research Record 2674. https://doi.org/10.1177/0361198120945696
- Duncan, M. (2019). *Would the replacement of park-and-ride facilities with
  transit-oriented development reduce vehicle kilometers traveled...* Transport Policy 81.
  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tranpol.2017.12.005

applicability.warn_message: Park-and-ride is most defensible in suburban, rural, and regional commute corridors where it shortens drive-alone trips.

strategies.name: Parking Cash-Out
strategies.short_description: Offering employees cash or equivalent benefits in lieu of a free parking space.
strategies.extended_description:
Parking cash-outs are the practice of offering employees cash or equivalent benefits in
lieu of a free parking space. Parking cash-outs encourage individuals to choose alternative
modes for commuting trips, especially when paired with free transit passes or other TDM
measures that reduce transportation costs for the user.

The effect of parking cash-outs will depend on the presence of alternative modes of
transportation and their ease of use. If alternative modes are accessible, easy to use, and
lower cost than driving, individuals may be more likely to choose to participate in a
parking cash-out.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for employer programs that offer employees cash or an
equivalent benefit when they forgo a free or subsidized parking space. This strategy
applies to commute trips and should be used only for employees who are eligible for an
employer-provided parking benefit. Double counting can occur if cash-out benefits are
already modeled under [Workplace Parking
Pricing](#/strategies/workplace_parking_pricing),
[Employee Commuting
Benefits](#/strategies/employee_commuting_benefits),
or [Commuter
Incentives](#/strategies/commute_incentives).
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-13 (parking price-elasticity chain)
strategies.formula: ΔCommuteVMT% = −clamp(|(cash_out / parking_cost) × −0.4 × eligible × veh_MS × p_drive × conv|, 0, 12%)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Offering cash in lieu of a free or subsidized parking space exposes the true cost of
parking and lets employees pocket the value if they don't drive, shifting commute trips off
single-occupancy driving. Following CAPCOA
[T-13 (Implement Employee Parking Cash-Out)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-13.pdf),
the cash-out amount is treated as a price signal applied to parking and run through the
parking price-elasticity → mode-share → vehicle-miles-traveled (VMT) chain:

`ΔVMT% = −(cash_out / avg_parking_cost) × −0.4 × pct_eligible × commute_vehicle_mode_share × pct_would_drive × trip_to_VMT`

using the parking-demand price elasticity of **−0.4** (Lehner & Peirson 2019). The commute
vehicle mode share comes from the area's observed commute mode share. "Percent eligible" is
the share of employees who *could* participate (usually 100%), not the share who actually
do.

The reduction is capped at the **~12% empirical ceiling** from Shoup's eight-employer
cash-out study (1997), corroborated by a ~12% single-occupancy reduction in a Twin Cities
seven-employer study (FHWA 2023).

> **Constants pending confirmation.** The CAPCOA T-13 fact sheet could not be read at
> implementation time. The "share of affected parking trips that would otherwise be driven"
> and the trip-to-VMT conversion are **placeholders** exposed in the code
> (`PARKING_CASHOUT_T13`); whether the elasticity applies to a price *ratio* (used here) or
> an absolute daily price is also unconfirmed. Confirm against the fact sheet before relying
> on the numbers. Outputs flag this.

**Sources**

- CAPCOA *Handbook*, Measure
  [T-13 (Implement Employee Parking Cash-Out)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-13.pdf).
- Lehner & Peirson (2019), parking price elasticity (−0.4).
- Shoup, D. (1997), *Evaluating the effects of cashing out employer-paid parking* (~12% VMT).
- FHWA (2023), *City-Level Parking Cash-Out and Commuter Benefits Ordinances*.

applicability.warn_message: Cash-out works where commuters have viable non-driving options; results use placeholder constants pending CAPCOA T-13 confirmation.

who actually take the cash-out.

strategies.name: Parking Fees and Curb Management
strategies.short_description: Price and manage on- and off-street public parking across an area to reduce auto trips and improve turnover.
strategies.extended_description:
Parking fees and curb management price public parking in areas such as metered on-street
spaces, municipal lots, or managed curb zones. Pricing helps manage limited parking so
spaces are more likely to be available for people who need them, while also encouraging
some commuters to consider lower-cost options such as transit, carpooling, biking,
walking, or other travel options.

The effect depends on the price, whether free parking is still available nearby, and the
quality of other possible travel options that avoid the need for parking.
strategies.guidance:
This strategy applies the price change to a share of area driving
specified by the user. For parking charged by employers, use [Workplace Parking
Pricing](#/strategies/workplace_parking_pricing).
For rates that change with demand, use [Dynamic Parking
Pricing](#/strategies/dynamic_parking_pricing).
strategies.method: Lehner & Peer (2019) parking demand elasticity (ε=−0.40), all trips
strategies.methodology_detail:
Charging for public parking that used to be free or cheap raises the cost of
driving to those destinations, so some trips are made another way or not at all,
reducing vehicle miles traveled (VMT). The larger the price increase and the more
of the area's driving it covers, the bigger the reduction, following CAPCOA
[T-24 (Implement Market Price Public Parking, On-Street)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-24.pdf)
and the parking-response relationship in Lehner & Peer (2019).

`ΔVMT% = %Δprice × ε × share_affected`

Where parking is free today, introducing a charge is treated as a meaningful price
increase. The estimate is most reliable for moderate price changes and overstates
the response to very large ones (above about a 50% increase).

applicability.warn_message: Priced public and curb parking is an urban tool with little application in lower-density areas where parking is free and plentiful.

strategies.name: Pedestrian Network Improvements
strategies.short_description: New and repaired sidewalks that close gaps in the pedestrian network, shifting short trips from driving to walking.
strategies.extended_description:
Pedestrian network improvements add new sidewalks and repair degraded or substandard ones,
closing gaps that make walking impractical. A more complete, comfortable pedestrian network
encourages people to walk for short trips that would otherwise be made by car, lowering
vehicle miles traveled.

The effect depends on how much the sidewalk network expands relative to the street network
and on how many nearby trips are short enough to walk. Sidewalk investments are most
effective in compact, mixed-use areas where destinations are close together and the main
barrier is a missing or broken pedestrian connection.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for projects that add or repair sidewalks within a study
area (about a 0.6-mile radius, a 6–10 minute walk, around the improvement). Measure
sidewalk length on both sides of the street: a 0.5-mile street with full coverage is 1.0
mile of sidewalk.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-18 (verbatim)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Adding sidewalk coverage shifts some short household trips from driving to walking,
following CAPCOA
[T-18 (Provide Pedestrian Network Improvement)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-18.pdf):

`ΔVMT% = ((C / B) − 1) × D`

where **B** is existing sidewalk length, **C** is sidewalk length with the measure (both
measured on both sides of the street within a ~0.6-mile study area), and **D = −0.05** is
the elasticity of household vehicle travel with respect to the sidewalk-to-street ratio
(Frank et al. 2011; Handy et al. 2014).

The reduction is capped at a **6.4% measure maximum**, derived from the share of vehicle
trips short enough to shift to walking (FHWA 2019). *Reviewer note:* the fact sheet
references a 3.4% figure in one location and 6.4% in the cap derivation and worked example;
6.4% is used here per the worked example, flagged for confirmation. The credit applies to
household vehicle travel; because the calculator does not carry a household-only VMT split,
it is applied to all-trip VMT and flagged accordingly.

*Worked example:* B = 9 miles, C = 10 miles → `((10/9) − 1) × −0.05 = −0.56%`.

**Sources**

- CAPCOA *Handbook* (2021), Measure
  [T-18 (Provide Pedestrian Network Improvement)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-18.pdf),
  pp. 133–136.
- Frank, L., et al. (2011). WSDOT Research Report WA-RD 765.1.
- Handy, S., et al. (2014). *Impacts of Pedestrian Strategies on Passenger Vehicle Use and
  GHG Emissions*. CARB.

strategies.name: Increased Residential Density
strategies.short_description: Increase housing units per acre to support shorter trips and more walking, biking, and transit use.
strategies.extended_description:
Increasing residential density adds dense residential development in places where
residents can reach jobs, services, transit, and everyday destinations with shorter
trips. The VMT reduction benefit is strongest when the development is convenient to key
destinations via walking, biking, and transit options. Dense housing alone, without
nearby destinations or multimodal infrastructure, will not provide significant VMT
reduction benefits.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for housing-focused rezoning or denser residential
development. To model a mix of homes and jobs, or a broader change in land use mix,
combine it with [Increased Employment
Density](#/strategies/employment_density).
strategies.method: Stevens (2016) residential VMT-density elasticity (ε=−0.22)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Placing more homes close to destinations shortens trips and makes walking,
biking, and transit more viable, which lowers vehicle miles traveled (VMT). A 1%
increase in residential density has been associated with about a 0.22% reduction
in VMT (Stevens 2016), the basis CAPCOA uses for
[T-1 (Increase Residential Density)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-1.pdf).
Housing density is a stronger lever than job density.

`ΔVMT% = Δres_density × ε_res`

To represent a change in the mix of land uses or a mixed-use development, combine
this strategy with Increase employment density.

applicability.warn_message: The density–driving relationship comes from urban and suburban areas; in rural areas, added density yields little reduction in driving or can increase trip lengths.

inputs.summary: The percent change in housing units per acre the project adds, compared with today's baseline for the project area.
inputs.source_note: your development program / site plan vs. local baseline (DOLA estimates, zoning)

for the project area. A project that doubles density is +100%. The Colorado
Department of Local Affairs (DOLA) housing estimates and local zoning references
(such as the New Zoning Atlas) can help you compare proposed density against
existing conditions.

Approximate benchmarks (people per square mile):

- Standard single-family suburb: ~3,000–5,000
- Downtown Denver (high-rise): ~13,000–16,000
- Capitol Hill, Denver's densest neighborhood: ~25,000

These are order-of-magnitude anchors; local figures vary with lot size,
building height, and household size.

strategies.name: Protected or Buffered Bike Lanes
strategies.short_description: New physically separated bike lanes on roads parallel to a corridor, accounting for ridable days and typical trip lengths.
strategies.extended_description:
Protected bike lanes have physical barriers such as curbs or posts between the bike
facility and roadway. Buffered bike lanes provide space between the bike facility and
the roadway but do not include physical barriers. Protected bike lanes are typically
considered more high-comfort due to their physically separated nature.

High-comfort bike facilities with strong connectivity to the larger bike network and key
destinations serve trips that could more reasonably be shifted from driving. Bikeways
with unsafe intersection crossings, missing connections or other issues may make biking
less appealing.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for separated bicycle facilities. Facilities that are
non-separated bike lanes or just sharrows should select the [Striped Bike Lanes,
Neighborhood Bikeways and
Sharrows](#/strategies/sharrows_bike_lanes)
strategy. The model also factors in seasonality when estimating bike ridership.
strategies.method: Adapted CAPCOA T-19-A
strategies.methodology_detail:
A protected lane gives people a comfortable enough route that some who would have
driven choose to bike instead, lowering vehicle miles traveled (VMT). The effect
grows with the share of nearby driving on the streets the lane parallels and with
the number of days a year that are comfortable for cycling, and it is adjusted for
the fact that bike trips are typically shorter than car trips, following CAPCOA
[T-19-A (Construct or Improve Bike Facility)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-19-a.pdf)
and [T-20 (Expand Bikeway Network)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-20.pdf),
using a +0.07 effect size.

`ΔVMT% = −%VMT_parallel × (annual_use_days / 365) × ε × L_bike / L_veh`

Local commute travel and trip lengths come from the area data; the number of
comfortable cycling days is estimated for the area from National Oceanic and
Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) climate records.

**Sources**

- CAPCOA, *Handbook for Analyzing Greenhouse Gas Emission Reductions* (2021),
  measures [T-19-A (Construct or Improve Bike Facility)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-19-a.pdf)
  and [T-20 (Expand Bikeway Network)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-20.pdf).
- [NOAA NCEI, 1991–2020 U.S. Daily Climate Normals](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/us-climate-normals)

inputs.label: Share of area VMT on parallel roadways
inputs.summary: The share of your area's driving carried on the street the new bike lane runs along and nearby parallel roads.
inputs.tooltip: Engineering judgment: share of the corridor's driving carried on the street the new bike lane runs on and nearby parallel roads.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of your area's driving that happens on the streets your new
bike lane runs alongside. A quick approach: identify the parallel street(s) the
lane serves, then judge what fraction of all local driving they carry. A
protected lane along a single arterial in a small area might be 5–15%; a lane
along a minor street might be 1–3%. If you have a travel demand model or traffic
counts, divide the driving on the parallel streets by total area driving. When
in doubt, start with the 5% default and adjust.

To check traffic on a specific street, CDOT's [Traffic Data Explorer](https://dtdapps.codot.gov/otis/trafficdata)
maps annual average daily traffic (AADT) counts for state highways statewide.

inputs.label: Annual ridable days
inputs.tooltip: Filled in from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) 1991-2020 climate records for your area. Adjust if you have a project-specific number.
inputs.instructions:
This is the number of days per year the weather is comfortable for cycling: a
daytime high between 32°F and 95°F with no rain or snow. You usually don't need
to look this up: the calculator fills it in from National Oceanic and Atmospheric
Administration (NOAA) climate records for your area. Only override it if you have
a local estimate, for example a community with an unusually long riding season.

strategies.name: Shared Micromobility
strategies.short_description: Shared bikes, e-bikes, or scooters available for short trips. How much driving they replace varies by device type.
strategies.extended_description:
Shared micromobility provides short-term access to shared bicycles, e-bikes, or scooters
for short trips and connections to transit. It is most useful in places where trips are
too long to walk comfortably but short enough that driving is not time or cost
effective.

The benefits of shared micromobility depend on how many micromobility trips replace car
trips rather than walking, transit, or personal bike trips. Systems located near
transit, campuses, downtowns, and dense neighborhoods generally have stronger potential,
especially when shared micromobility devices are easy to find and parking is well
managed.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for launching or expanding a shared fleet. Enter how
much of the population can reach a vehicle before and after the project, and select the
device type that matches the system.
strategies.method: Effect-size estimate (adapted CAPCOA T-22-A / T-22-B / T-22-C; NACTO trip-substitution research)
strategies.methodology_detail:
When a shared bike, e-bike, or scooter is within easy reach, some trips that would
have been made by car are made on the device instead, lowering vehicle miles
traveled (VMT). The reduction depends on how many more people can reach the system
and the device type, since each type replaces car trips at a different rate: pedal
bikes about 20%, e-bikes about 35%, and scooters about 39% (McQueen et al. 2020;
Fitch et al. 2021).

`ΔVMT% = −Δaccess × micro_trips × sub_ratio × L_micro / (veh_trips × L_veh)`

This estimate is adapted from CAPCOA
[T-22-A (pedal bikeshare)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-22-a.pdf),
[T-22-B (electric bikeshare)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-22-b.pdf),
and [T-22-C (scootershare)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-22-c.pdf),
with trip data from the National Association of City Transportation Officials
(NACTO).

applicability.warn_message: Shared bike and scooter systems need urban densities to attract enough trips and are rarely viable below them.

inputs.label: Mode type
inputs.summary: The device type that matches the system (pedal bikeshare, e-bike share, or scooter share), which sets how often it replaces a car trip.
inputs.source_note: your system plan or vendor / operator agreement
inputs.tooltip: Determines the default substitution ratio.
inputs.instructions:
Pick the device type that matches the system. It sets the auto-substitution
ratio: e-bikes and scooters replace car trips more often than pedal bikes, so
they yield a larger VMT effect for the same number of trips.

inputs.label: % population with access today
inputs.summary: The share of the area's population that already lives within an easy walk (about a quarter mile) of an existing dock, station, or service zone. Enter 0% if none today.
inputs.source_note: your existing service map / station locations
inputs.tooltip: Estimate of households within walking distance (≈¼ mi) of an existing dock/station.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of the area's population that already lives within an easy
walk (about ¼ mile) of an existing dock, station, or service zone. If there is
no system today, this is 0%.

inputs.label: % population with access after
inputs.summary: The share of the area's population within an easy walk of the system after the deployment or expansion is complete.
inputs.source_note: your proposed deployment plan / service-area map
inputs.tooltip: Estimate after the proposed deployment is complete.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of the population within an easy walk of the system after
the deployment or expansion. The difference from today's access drives the
reduction: a citywide dockless permit reaches far more people than a few
downtown stations.

strategies.name: Striped Bike Lanes, Neighborhood Bikeways and Sharrows
strategies.short_description: Lower-grade on-street bike infrastructure (sharrows, painted lanes) applied across an area, raising bike mode share by a documented effect size.
strategies.extended_description:
Bike lanes are facilities that do not have separation between the roadway and the
bikeway. They are typically defined by pavement markings, such as a painted line, rather
than by curbs, posts or other physical separation.

Sharrows, or shared lane markings, are pavement markings that indicate where bicyclists
may ride within a shared travel lane. They can help alert drivers to expect bicyclists
along a corridor, but they do not provide any significant comfort and safety
improvements for those riding bikes.

Neighborhood bikeways are travel lanes shared by vehicles and bicyclists, but they are
an improvement over sharrows because they include additional intersection and mid-block
safety measures to reduce vehicle speeds and volumes.

The relative comfortability and safety of each facility type depends on vehicle speed,
vehicle volume, connectivity to the larger bike network, and other corridor factors.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for bike lanes, sharrows or neighborhood bikeways. For
physically separated bikeways, use [Protected or Buffered Bike
Lanes](#/strategies/separated_bike_lanes).
For workplace amenities such as bicycle parking, showers, and lockers, use [Workplace
Bicycle
Amenities](#/strategies/end_of_trip_facilities).
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-19-A / T-20 (bike facility / network expansion), area_vmt scope
strategies.methodology_detail:
Making streets more bike-friendly encourages more people to bike for trips they
would otherwise drive, lowering vehicle miles traveled (VMT). Sharrows and painted
lanes raise the share of trips made by bike by about 15% within the area they
cover, following CAPCOA
[T-19-A (Construct or Improve Bike Facility)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-19-a.pdf)
and [T-20 (Expand Bikeway Network)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-20.pdf).
Because bike trips are typically shorter than car trips, the calculator accounts
for that when converting the added bike trips into driving avoided.

`ΔVMT% = −scope_share × L_bike × (bike_MS × adj) / (L_veh × auto_MS)`

This uses the same bike effect as [Workplace Bicycle
Amenities](https://high-street.bitbucket.io/cdot_tdm_calculator/#/strategies/end_of_trip_facilities),
applied across an area rather than to commuters at a worksite.

applicability.warn_message: On-street bike treatments shift the most trips in denser, walkable areas; the effect is limited in rural areas.

inputs.label: Share of area VMT treated
inputs.summary: The share of your area's driving carried on the streets that will receive the new sharrows or painted bike lanes.
inputs.tooltip: Share of area driving on the streets receiving sharrows / painted lanes.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of your area's driving carried on the streets that get the
new markings or painted lanes. Identify the treated streets, then judge what
fraction of local driving they carry. A network of sharrows across many streets
covers more than a single painted lane.

To check traffic on a specific street, CDOT's [Traffic Data Explorer](https://dtdapps.codot.gov/otis/trafficdata)
maps annual average daily traffic (AADT) counts for state highways statewide.

strategies.notes: Split from bike_mode_share_booster. Engine: strategy_bike_mode_share_booster (scope=area_vmt).

strategies.name: Telework and Flexible Work Schedules
strategies.short_description: Hybrid or full-remote work policies that eliminate commute trips on telework days.
strategies.extended_description:
Flexible work schedules and telework policies reduce commute travel by changing when,
how often, or whether employees commute to their workplace. Telework eliminates commute
trips on days where employees work from home, while compressed work schedules, staggered
shifts, and flexible start times can also reduce peak period commute pressure.

The largest VMT reductions occur for eligible employees who would otherwise drive long
distances. Outcomes depend on job eligibility, participation, and how employers manage
their policies.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for hybrid or fully remote policies and compressed work
weeks. Enter the realistic average number of days worked from home, not the maximum
allowed by the policy, because actual use is usually lower.
strategies.method: Direct commute-trip elimination on telework days
strategies.methodology_detail:
When eligible employees work from home, their commute trips disappear on those
days, directly reducing commute vehicle miles traveled (VMT). The reduction is the
share of workers who can telework multiplied by the average share of the work week
they do.

`Δcommute_VMT% = −%eligible × (telework_days / 5)`

No extra effect size is applied; each skipped commute counts as avoided driving.
(The 2021 CAPCOA Handbook no longer lists telework as its own measure; it treats
telework as one part of a commute trip reduction program.) The default share of
workers who can telework is estimated from the area's mix of jobs, drawn from
American Community Survey (ACS) data.

**Caveat: induced (rebound) travel.** This estimate captures only the commute trips
that are eliminated on telework days, so it should be read as a *commute-trip
reduction* and may overstate net VMT savings. A growing body of research finds that
telework can induce offsetting travel: people make additional non-commute trips during
the day, and the weaker tie to a daily commute can lead some households to choose homes
farther from work, lengthening the trips they do make. The net effect on total VMT is
uncertain and context-dependent, and in some cases telework can increase overall
driving. Treat the figure here as an upper bound on commute-VMT savings rather than a
guaranteed reduction in total VMT.

inputs.label: Telework-eligible workforce
inputs.summary: The share of the area's workers in jobs that can be done remotely; office and professional roles raise it, manual roles lower it.
inputs.source_note: your employer's job mix (or the area's occupation mix)
inputs.tooltip: ACS occupation-mix-derived. Office/professional roles → higher; manual/in-person → lower.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of the area's workers in jobs that can be done remotely. The
default is based on the local mix of jobs: office and professional roles raise
it, manual and in-person roles lower it. Adjust it if you know the specific
employers involved: a single office employer is mostly able to telework, a
warehouse is not.

inputs.label: Days/week teleworked
inputs.summary: The average number of days per week eligible employees actually work remotely, not the policy maximum (typical hybrid is 2-3 days).
inputs.source_note: your employer's telework policy and actual participation
inputs.tooltip: Average across eligible workers. Typical hybrid = 2-3 days.
inputs.instructions:
Enter the average number of days per week eligible employees actually work
remotely, not the policy maximum. A typical hybrid policy lands around 2–3
days once you account for staff who come in more often than allowed.

strategies.name: TMO Coverage Expansion
strategies.short_description: Bring more employers under a Transportation Management Organization that coordinates TDM programs across a district.
strategies.extended_description:
A transportation management organization or association is a formal partnership that
coordinates travel demand management programs for a defined area, corridor, district, or
employment center. TMOs provide shared staff capacity, employer outreach, program
administration, and coordination that individual employers or jurisdictions may not be
able to sustain alone.

The effect depends on the number of commuters reached, the strength of the services
provided, and the availability of practical alternatives to driving alone.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy to model the creation of a new TMO or the expansion of
an existing one. The benefit should be based on the additional share of the workforce or
travel market covered by active TMO services.
strategies.method: CAPCOA T-5 (voluntary CTR) midpoint, 4% per eligible
strategies.methodology_detail:
A Transportation Management Organization helps more employees shift out of driving
alone by coordinating commute programs across many worksites. Each newly covered
worker is credited with about a 4% reduction in commute vehicle miles traveled
(VMT), following the voluntary commute trip reduction evidence in CAPCOA
[T-5 (Implement Commute Trip Reduction Program, Voluntary)](https://www.caleemod.com/documents/handbook/ch_3_transportation/measure_t-5.pdf).

`Δcommute_VMT% = −(share_after − share_before) × r_CTR`

Only the *change* in coverage counts, so enter the share of the workforce the
organization covers today and the share it will cover after the expansion.

applicability.warn_message: Transportation Management Organizations rely on a cluster of employers and commute alternatives, which are limited in rural areas.

inputs.label: Workforce coverage today
inputs.summary: The share of the area's employees who already work at TMO-member worksites today (0% for a brand-new TMO).
inputs.source_note: current TMO membership rolls vs. area employment
inputs.tooltip: Share of area employees at TMO-member workplaces.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of the area's employees who already work at TMO-member
worksites today. For a brand-new TMO this is 0%; for an expansion, use the
current membership's share of area employment.

inputs.label: Workforce coverage after
inputs.summary: The target share of area employees who will work at TMO-member worksites after the new or expanded organization is in place.
inputs.source_note: your TMO expansion plan / membership targets
inputs.tooltip: Target share after new TMO is established or existing TMO grows.
inputs.instructions:
Estimate the share of area employees who will work at TMO-member worksites
after the new or expanded organization is in place. The difference between
this and today's coverage is what drives the reduction.

strategies.name: Traffic Calming
strategies.short_description: Street design measures (e.g., speed humps, curb extensions) that slow vehicle speeds and improve safety.
strategies.extended_description:
Traffic calming helps to reduce vehicle speeds and improve the safety and comfort of people
walking, biking, rolling, and accessing transit. While traffic calming alone will likely
have little impact on VMT reductions, it makes trips completed by active transportation
safer. Traffic calming can include speed humps, curb extensions, chicanes, lane narrowing,
median islands, mini roundabouts, and other changes to the streetscape that slow vehicle
traffic and improve perceived and actual safety for users walking, biking, or rolling.

The effect of traffic calming will vary based on roadway context, surrounding land use, and
the strength of the active transportation network. Traffic calming is most effective when
paired with sidewalks, crossings, bike facilities, and transit access, especially in
locations where high vehicle speeds or wide crossing distances discourage individuals from
choosing alternative transportation modes.
strategies.guidance:
Use this strategy for street design measures that slow vehicle speeds and
improve comfort for people walking, biking, rolling, or accessing transit. Traffic calming
should generally be applied on local streets, station access routes, school routes, or
other low- to medium-volume corridors where speed and safety are barriers to non-driving
trips.
strategies.method: CAPCOA 2010 SDT-2 (legacy)
strategies.methodology_detail:
Traffic calming is credited using the 2010 CAPCOA measure
[SDT-2 (Traffic Calming Measures)](https://www.aqmd.gov/docs/default-source/ceqa/handbook/capcoa-quantifying-greenhouse-gas-mitigation-measures.pdf),
the only published method that assigns traffic calming a standalone VMT credit. The
reduction scales SDT-2's documented 0.25%–1.00% range by how much of the project's
network receives calming, taken as the average of the share of streets and the share of
intersections with improvements (beyond what the jurisdiction already requires):

`coverage = mean(streets_with_calming / total_streets, intersections_with_calming / total_intersections)`

`ΔVMT% = −(0.25% + coverage × (1.00% − 0.25%))`, capped at the 1.00% measure maximum.

If only one of the two coverage measures is available, that one is used rather than
averaging it against a zero.

**Legacy note:** In the 2021/2024 CAPCOA Handbook, traffic calming was reclassified as
the *non-quantified* supporting measure T-35 and folded conceptually into pedestrian
network improvements; it no longer carries a discrete VMT credit. This implementation is
retained per CDOT's request for a standalone traffic-calming credit and is flagged as a
legacy method. Avoid double-counting with the Pedestrian Network Improvements strategy.

**Sources**

- CAPCOA, *Quantifying Greenhouse Gas Mitigation Measures* (2010), Measure SDT-2, p. 190.
- SMAQMD, *Recommended Guidance for Land Use Emission Reductions v3.0* (SDT-2 coverage
  variable definitions).

applicability.warn_message: Traffic calming carries only a small, legacy VMT credit (≤1%) and is most effective paired with active-transportation investments.

inputs.label: Streets with calming improvements
inputs.summary: The number of streets or street segments in the project area that will receive traffic-calming features beyond what your jurisdiction already requires.
inputs.source_note: your project design drawings / plan set
inputs.tooltip: Number of streets receiving traffic-calming features beyond jurisdiction requirements.
inputs.instructions:
Count the streets (or street segments) in the project area that will receive
traffic-calming features (speed humps, curb extensions, chicanes, lane narrowing,
etc.) beyond what your jurisdiction already requires.

inputs.label: Total streets in project area
inputs.summary: The total number of streets or street segments in the project area, used to work out the share that receive calming.
inputs.source_note: your project area map or GIS street layer
inputs.tooltip: Total number of streets in the project area, used to compute coverage.
inputs.instructions:
Count the total streets (or street segments) in the project area so the calculator
can work out the share that receive calming.

inputs.label: Intersections with calming improvements
inputs.summary: The number of intersections in the project area that will receive calming features such as mini roundabouts, raised crossings, or curb extensions.
inputs.source_note: your project design drawings / plan set
inputs.tooltip: Number of intersections receiving traffic-calming features.
inputs.instructions:
Count the intersections receiving calming features such as mini roundabouts, raised
crossings, or curb extensions. Leave at 0 if you are only tracking street coverage.

inputs.label: Total intersections in project area
inputs.summary: The total number of intersections in the project area, used to work out the share that receive calming.
inputs.source_note: your project area map or GIS intersection layer
inputs.tooltip: Total number of intersections in the project area, used to compute coverage.
inputs.instructions:
Count the total intersections in the project area. If you provide only street counts
(or only intersection counts), the calculator uses whichever coverage measure is
available rather than averaging against a zero.
